domainCoverage.synopsis: System architecture comprises the decisions that are expensive to reverse. This volume explores decoupled message streaming, bounded contexts, and circuit breakers.

theory.overview: Software architecture establishes the fundamental structural decisions, component boundaries, and communication contracts that govern how systems evolve. Sound architecture optimizes for changeability, testability, and clear ownership.
theory.whyItMatters: Architectural mistakes are 100x more expensive to reverse once deployed across multiple production services.
keyMechanisms: Conway's Law: System interfaces will inevitably mirror team communication structures.
High cohesion and loose coupling maximize independent team velocity.
Automated fitness functions in CI prevent progressive architecture erosion.

theory.overview: Decomposing monolithic systems requires strategic discipline. The Strangler Fig pattern and Modular Monolith principles allow teams to decompose software without high-risk big-bang rewrites.
theory.whyItMatters: Decomposing systems along naive entity boundaries produces chatty network calls, distributed joins, and cascading latency traps.
keyMechanisms: A modular monolith is the safest starting point for most engineering teams.
The Strangler Fig pattern replaces legacy monoliths incrementally with zero downtime.
Each microservice must own its private datastore; direct database sharing is strictly prohibited.

theory.overview: Strategic Domain-Driven Design (DDD) provides the architectural framework to partition complex enterprise software into cohesive Bounded Contexts with unambiguous Ubiquitous Language.
theory.whyItMatters: Without bounded contexts, domain terms become overloaded and models bleed together, leading to unmaintainable spaghetti code.
keyMechanisms: A model only has meaning within its explicit Bounded Context.
Anti-Corruption Layers isolate modern core domains from messy legacy dependencies.
Focus maximum engineering effort on the Core Domain that delivers competitive advantage.

keyMechanisms: Aggregates enforce transactional invariants; state outside an aggregate converges eventually.
Value objects are immutable and self-validating, eliminating invalid domain states.
Repositories emulate in-memory collections, shielding the domain from SQL/ORM details.

theory.overview: Hexagonal and Clean Architectures isolate business rules from external technology choices. Databases, web frameworks, and messaging brokers become swappable implementation details.
theory.whyItMatters: Coupling core business logic to ORM entities or web frameworks makes migrating frameworks or upgrading libraries a nightmare.
keyMechanisms: The Dependency Rule: Dependencies point strictly inward towards domain logic.
Business logic knows nothing about HTTP, SQL, JSON, or external SDKs.
In-memory mock adapters allow end-to-end business testing in milliseconds without spinning up databases.

theory.whyItMatters: Updating current database state in-place destroys historical context, making temporal debugging and financial auditing impossible.
keyMechanisms: Commands represent intent (can be rejected); Events represent facts (cannot be changed).
CQRS decouples write optimization (normalized) from read optimization (denormalized).
Event sourcing treats the append-only event log as the single source of truth.

keyMechanisms: API Gateways decouple internal microservice implementations from public client contracts.
Consumer-Driven Contract tests prevent breaking API updates from reaching production.
Service mesh sidecars handle mTLS, retries, and telemetry without polluting business code.

theory.overview: Serverless architectures eliminate operational server management and scale elastically from zero to tens of thousands of concurrent executions in seconds.
theory.whyItMatters: Unconstrained serverless concurrency creates massive thundering herds that crush traditional relational databases and downstream APIs.
keyMechanisms: Serverless functions must remain strictly stateless; memory state is destroyed between invocations.
Control concurrency limits using reserved concurrency to protect downstream database pools.
Use Step Functions for stateful multi-step sagas rather than chaining functions synchronously.

theory.whyItMatters: Attempting to run distributed ACID transactions across microservices using 2PC leads to brittle, blocking systems with catastrophic availability drops.
keyMechanisms: Each service owns its private data; cross-service data access happens strictly through APIs or events.
Sagas achieve atomicity eventually through compensating actions.
Transactional Outbox ensures zero lost events between relational database commits and Kafka.

keyMechanisms: Move slow, heavy operations (emails, analytics, image processing) off the request thread into async queues.
Multi-tier caches absorb 95%+ of read traffic, protecting primary relational databases.
Read-write splitting scales read capacity but requires tolerance for replica lag.

theory.overview: Resilient architectures are designed under the assumption that hardware, network, and software dependencies will fail continuously. Bulkheads, circuit breakers, and timeouts isolate failure blast radius.
theory.whyItMatters: Omitting timeouts on network calls causes threads to block indefinitely, exhausting application server worker pools in seconds.
keyMechanisms: Every network call must have an explicit connection and read timeout.
Circuit breakers fail fast, allowing failing dependencies to recover without being overwhelmed.
Bulkheads ensure a failure in one feature cannot starve resources for the entire platform.

domainDeepDive.whatIsThisDomain: Software architecture comprises the high-level structural decisions, boundary definitions, and communication contracts that govern how systems are built, decomposed, and evolved. It establishes how business capabilities map to software components, how state and transactional ownership are partitioned across domain boundaries, and how non-functional requirements (scalability, security, maintainability, and fault isolation) are satisfied throughout the software lifecycle.
domainDeepDive.whyItMatters: Software architecture encompasses the decisions that are perilous and expensive to change once systems reach production. An architecture misaligned with organizational domain boundaries creates distributed monoliths—architectures that suffer the extreme operational complexity of distributed networks while retaining the catastrophic coupling of monolithic systems. Correct architecture provides clear boundaries of change, enabling dozens of autonomous teams to ship features continuously without coordination bottlenecks.
domainDeepDive.keyTakeaway: Optimize architecture for loose coupling, clear data ownership, and reversibility. The best architecture is not the one that predicts the future, but the one that makes changing your mind inexpensive.
coreArchitectureRules: Conway's Law Invariant: Software system architectures inevitably mirror the communication structures of the organizations that design them. Align system boundaries with autonomous team boundaries.

Single Source of Truth & Data Sovereignty: Each microservice or bounded context must exclusively own its underlying database schema. Direct database sharing across service boundaries is strictly prohibited.

The End-to-End Argument: Lower-level system components cannot anticipate all higher-level semantic requirements. Crucial application guarantees (such as transactional deduplication and data integrity) must be validated end-to-end at the application layer.

Postel's Robustness Principle: Be conservative in what you send, and liberal in what you accept. Services must tolerate additive schema changes (backward and forward compatibility) without deployment locks.

Fault Domain Isolation: Every architectural boundary must establish an explicit fault barrier. Failure in an analytics or recommendation subsystem must never degrade core checkout or authentication paths.

failureModes.name: The Distributed Monolith Trap
failureModes.description: Decomposing an application into 40 microservices that share a single relational database and require synchronous lockstep deployments, multiplying network latency without delivering team autonomy.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce strict domain boundaries using Domain-Driven Design (DDD). Decouple schemas into private datastores and communicate exclusively through versioned APIs or event streams.

failureModes.name: Chatty Distributed Query Cascades (N+1 Across Microservices)
failureModes.description: A frontend endpoint calls an aggregator service, which in turn performs sequential loops of RPC calls to multiple downstream microservices to assemble a single response, multiplying latency by N.
failureModes.mitigation: Employ CQRS read-model projections, GraphQL Federation with batching (DataLoader), or asynchronous materialized views populated via event streams.

failureModes.name: Schema Drift & Breaking Contract Deployments
failureModes.description: A producer service modifies an API response field or deletes an enum value, instantly breaking hundreds of downstream consumer services that lacked contract tests.
failureModes.mitigation: Implement consumer-driven contract testing (Pact) in CI pipelines and enforce schema evolution registries (Protobuf/Avro) that prohibit breaking field deletions.

failureModes.name: Shared Database Anti-Pattern
failureModes.description: Multiple services run direct SQL queries against tables owned by another team. Schema migrations by one team silently crash background workers in other domains.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce API encapsulation. Convert shared tables into private domain models accessible only via gRPC/REST APIs or published domain events.

whenToUse: Large engineering organizations with multiple autonomous product teams needing independent deployment cadences.
Complex business domains with distinct sub-domains (e.g. payment processing, order fulfillment, catalog search) that scale and evolve at different speeds.
Systems requiring disparate non-functional characteristics (e.g. streaming telemetry requiring high write throughput vs checkout requiring strict ACID linearizability).
Applications transitioning from a monolithic legacy core to modular services using Strangler Fig migrations.
whenNotToUse: Early-stage MVPs where business requirements and domain boundaries are rapidly shifting weekly; a well-factored Modular Monolith is 10x faster to iterate on.
Small development teams (fewer than 10-15 engineers) where the operational tax of microservices (Kubernetes, service meshes, distributed tracing) drains development velocity.
Workloads with deeply intertwined relational queries requiring low-latency transactions across hundreds of foreign keys.
CRUD applications with minimal business logic that simply proxy requests to a relational database.

tradeOffs.pro: Modular monoliths provide zero network latency, single-repository refactoring, and simple atomic database transactions.
tradeOffs.con: All modules share a single deployment runtime, scaling envelope, and technology stack, limiting deployment independence for large teams.

tradeOffs.pro: Centralized orchestrators (Temporal / Step Functions) provide explicit, easily audited state machines and end-to-end visibility.
tradeOffs.con: Orchestrators create a centralized coupling point and can become an architectural bottleneck if overused.

tradeOffs.pro: gRPC delivers high-efficiency binary serialization (Protobuf) and typed contracts ideal for internal East-West microservice traffic.
tradeOffs.con: gRPC requires specialized tooling, lacks native browser support without grpc-web proxies, and is harder to inspect than JSON/REST.

productionScenarios.title: Strangler Fig Migration of Legacy Core Banking
productionScenarios.scenario: A 15-year-old monolithic core banking application blocked cloud migration and took 6 hours to build and deploy. Downtime risk was unacceptable.
productionScenarios.outcome: Implemented an API Gateway routing layer that intercepted incoming customer traffic, redirecting new loan origination flows to modern microservices while strangling legacy modules incrementally, achieving zero downtime across a 14-month phased rollout.

productionScenarios.title: CQRS Read-Optimized View for E-Commerce Catalog
productionScenarios.scenario: High-traffic Black Friday sales caused massive database lock contention on inventory tables because write transactions blocked millions of read queries.
productionScenarios.outcome: Split write commands from read queries using CQRS. Write commands update the relational inventory source of truth, while an event bus projects changes into read-optimized Elasticsearch indices, cutting catalog latency from 450ms to 9ms.

coreChallenges.title: Conway's Law & Team Boundaries
coreChallenges.explanation: System designs inevitably mirror the communication structures of the organizations that design them. Misaligned organizational boundaries produce mismatched system interfaces and cross-team deployment bottlenecks.

coreChallenges.title: Microservices Decomposition & Data Coupling
coreChallenges.explanation: Decomposing a system along entity boundaries rather than transaction and domain boundaries creates chatty distributed joins, distributed transactions, and cascading latency traps.

coreChallenges.title: Bounded Contexts & Ubiquitous Language
coreChallenges.explanation: A customer in billing is fundamentally different from a customer in shipping. Without explicit Domain-Driven Design (DDD) context mappings, shared models bleed across domains, creating unmaintainable dependencies.

coreChallenges.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Coupling
coreChallenges.explanation: Synchronous RPC cascades availability failures across downstream services. Asynchronous event-driven choreography isolates failures and decouples services in time, space, and deployment cadence.
